## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

\begin{marginfigure}
\mlagentstack{17}{17}{17}{17}{16}{16}
\end{marginfigure}

_Why can individually tested components still leave an agent's task unfinished or its effects unaccounted for?_

An autonomous agent unites disparate systems disciplines—foundation models, memory hierarchies, isolated execution sandboxes, transactional event logs, and formal verification—into a single closed-loop control architecture. Each individual component can satisfy its local unit tests, yet the integrated system can still fail if the contracts connecting them are ungrounded or ambiguous. The core challenge of agentic systems engineering is not maximizing model parameter counts or writing elaborate prompts, but designing the deterministic harness that guides, bounds, and verifies stochastic cognition. Across a trajectory horizon, carried working state, and delegated authority, reliable autonomy is achieved only when the runtime enforces invariant closure at every system boundary.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

\newpage

:::

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Trace an incident-remediation trajectory, identifying the owner and record of each consequential transition
- Translate a task contract into bounds and acceptance requirements proportionate to its horizon, state, and authority
- Diagnose state and evidence mismatches at subsystem boundaries using the authority and lifetime of each record
- Resolve an uncertain external action without confusing a lost response with permission to repeat its effect
- Select a system intervention using attributed failures, outcome evidence, and its full deployment cost
- Construct a safety case that connects scoped claims to arguments, evidence, assumptions, and residual uncertainty
- Distinguish assistance with specifications from authority to adopt them and accept the resulting task

:::
## Answers to the Three Questions {#sec-vol3-conclusion-questions}

The introduction to this book posed three foundational architectural questions that every subsequent chapter has addressed in part. With the complete system architecture now assembled, each question admits a concise engineering answer, and each answer represents a concrete design claim that this concluding chapter tests against a live operational workload.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The three foundational architectural questions governing agentic design are established in @sec-vol3-intro-questions.
:::

The first question asked when an adaptive, model-directed loop earns its cost over a deterministic workflow. The answer cannot be settled globally across an entire application; it must be resolved at each individual decision point by measuring the cost per accepted task under a fixed specification contract. A model should direct the next action only where interpreting dynamic, unstructured evidence improves the task acceptance rate by a larger factor than the added inference calls increase the cost of an attempt. Deterministic software should govern everywhere else. Evaluated by this metric, dynamic model loops belong strictly at phases such as root-cause diagnosis, where the next diagnostic transition cannot be enumerated in advance, while deterministic control structures manage the predictable orchestration surrounding them.

The second question asked what operational machinery must surround the model. The answer is strictly proportional to the task's exposure profile across state, authority, and execution horizon. Managing state requires selectively retrieved context, explicitly budgeted serving state, and durable audit records that preserve source authority. Governing authority demands typed, mediated action interfaces, definitive effect settlement before any retry loop can execute, and process containment enforced within the execution substrate beneath the model. Managing horizon requires a supervisory harness that bounds the total trajectory, a write-ahead log of intent recorded before committing each external side effect, and compensating workflows capable of mitigating actions that cannot be reversed. A read-only lookup requires little of this protective scaffolding, whereas an autonomous remediation agent operating on live production systems demands all of it.

The third question asked how operators verify that a task has actually succeeded. The answer requires objective evidence collected from an authoritative endpoint that directly monitors the target system, evaluated against an explicit contract adopted by system owners before execution began. This verification must satisfy a pre-declared closure evidence level, with any residual uncertainty explicitly quantified and assigned to an accountable owner. A model's self-generated report—no matter how coherent or persuasive—never serves as evidence, because a component executing within the loop cannot certify its own output. Stated as an operational acceptance rule, this is the discipline of invariant closure (principle \ref{pri-invariant-closure}).

Each of these principles is straightforward to state for an isolated component, but maintaining them across subsystem boundaries represents the primary failure mode of agentic architectures. Individually tested services routinely drop an in-flight task when state, authority, and verification handoffs cross architectural seams. To demonstrate how these three answers hold under operational conditions, this chapter evaluates them across a complete incident trajectory handled by the autonomous remediation agent—our lighthouse system that exercises state, authority, and horizon exposure simultaneously. The analysis traces this live incident through the system (@sec-vol3-conclusion-capstone), translates its operational obligations into an enforceable contract envelope (@sec-vol3-conclusion-envelope), tracks state persistence and evidence propagation across memory subsystems (@sec-vol3-conclusion-memory), and governs side-effecting actions within a defensive execution harness (@sec-vol3-conclusion-execution). It then evaluates when production failures justify modifying the underlying system (@sec-vol3-conclusion-adaptation) and consolidates these runtime mechanisms into an end-to-end safety case (@sec-vol3-conclusion-safety). Finally, the chapter examines the fundamental frontiers that remain unresolved (@sec-vol3-conclusion-frontiers), confronts the irreducible boundary that no software system can close autonomously (@sec-vol3-conclusion-brooks), and takes a last look at the machine this book has built.

## One Incident Through the System {#sec-vol3-conclusion-capstone}

A database service triggers a query-latency alert shortly after a configuration change. An automated remediation agent inspects telemetry, correlates logs, and proposes reverting to the previous known-good settings. The human operator approves the rollback, but the configuration endpoint drops the network connection before returning an acknowledgment. At this moment, the system faces a classic distributed systems dilemma: did the mutation take effect? No fluent textual explanation from a language model can answer that question. If the runtime interprets the timeout as a failure and retries under a fresh operation identifier, it risks executing the mutation twice. If it optimistically assumes success, it risks closing an incident while degraded queries continue to impact production. If it simply halts, it leaves a live production change in an unverified state with no entity accountable for it. Each failure mode arises by default when every component satisfies its local unit contract, yet no system component owns the distributed boundary between them.[^fn-endpoint-acceptance-argument]

[^fn-endpoint-acceptance-argument]: **End-to-End Argument**: @saltzer1984endtoend demonstrated that functions requiring complete correctness, such as reliable data delivery, can only be completely implemented with knowledge held at the endpoints of a system; lower-layer mechanisms optimize performance but cannot guarantee end-to-end correctness. Agentic task completion adheres to the exact same logic. An intermediate success report from a tool or model call cannot establish operational acceptance; only the principal holding the end-to-end task contract can verify completion against direct systems evidence. \index{End-to-end argument!task acceptance}

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/hsa_locator_hsa.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="H·S·A locator with all three axes, Horizon, State, and Authority, highlighted in purple."}

*Horizon, state, and authority return together, and the runtime closes each on one trajectory.*
:::

This concrete incident, `incident_42` on database service `db_primary_01`, represents the operational workload of our remediation agent (lighthouse \ref{lhs-vol3-remediation-agent}) and supplies the book's capstone synthesis. The remediation agent serves as our irreversible actor: it operates over a bounded horizon, mutates shared production state, and exercises real authority over a live service. Tracing this single trajectory—from initial diagnostic telemetry through operator approval, execution dispatch, and terminal acceptance—provides an anchor for the remainder of this chapter. At every transition, the engineering criterion remains constant: the system must deterministically record what it proposed, what permissions were granted, what physical effects occurred, what evidence validates the outcome, and which principal bears ongoing responsibility. Building an agentic machine learning system means guaranteeing that these accounts are durable and verifiable. In this architecture, the managed database service owns its active configuration, the runtime orchestrator owns execution and control decisions, and the accepting authority verifies whether post-remediation evidence satisfies the delegated operational contract.

The incident lifecycle begins under `incident_contract_v1`, which grants bounded diagnostic read access and establishes formal gates for proposing, approving, and validating configuration mutations. Initial privileges are strictly observational. The runtime provisions `read_scope_42` to query authorized service endpoints, ensuring that telemetry gathering cannot inadvertently trigger state changes or be coerced into production writes. Throughout this trace, identifiers such as `read_scope_42` denote durable local record keys rather than opaque cryptographic hashes.

Next, the context manager gathers the initial latency alert, recent time-series metrics, active configuration parameters, and relevant runbook sections into an auditable manifest, `context_manifest_42`. Every observation in this manifest records its originating source, a version tag when available, and a precise ingestion timestamp. Here, a practical systems hazard appears: while the retrieved runbook suggests a memory-pool misconfiguration, that document might describe a previous software deployment. By diffing the runbook recommendations against the active production configuration (`config_v7`) and current telemetry, the agent formulates a diagnostic hypothesis. Additional diagnostic queries—strictly constrained by the task's remaining call budget—must corroborate this hypothesis against alternative explanations such as downstream network congestion or disk saturation.

When the diagnostic evidence converges on a known regression, the model emits `change_request_42`, which specifies the target configuration keys, the desired values, and the expected baseline version `config_v7`. In accordance with incident change policy, an authorized human operator reviews the proposed diff and issues `approval_42`. This credential explicitly binds the operator's digital signature to the request identifier, the target host, the exact payload parameters, the prerequisite baseline `config_v7`, and a strict expiration window. Critically, this approval binding records permission for the designated operation rather than performing the mutation itself, covering that exact payload and nothing broader. The model drafts the operational rationale, but an untrusted model cannot grant itself execution authority. Prior to network dispatch, the runtime action gate rechecks operator authorization, verifies payload integrity against the approval signature, inspects expiration deadlines, confirms resource quotas, and evaluates runtime preconditions. If an operator revokes the ticket or the model generates an altered proposal, the original approval immediately invalidates rather than silently applying to a mutated repair payload.[^fn-complete-mediation-gate]

[^fn-complete-mediation-gate]: **Complete Mediation**: @saltzer1975 established complete mediation as a fundamental systems protection principle: every access to every protected object must be checked for authority at the moment of access rather than relying on cached decisions. An operator approval granted minutes before execution represents an earlier authorization check; the action gate revalidates identity, credentials, expiry, and payload invariants immediately before dispatch. \index{Complete mediation!action gate}

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Rechecking an approved request's digest, expiry, budget, and authorization at the dispatch boundary is established in @sec-vol3-agent-harness-dispatch-rechecks.
:::

Even a thorough pre-dispatch check cannot protect against time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU) races if a peer operator modifies database settings in the sub-second interval between the gate check and network arrival. The database configuration endpoint closes this distributed concurrency window using an atomic compare-and-swap or expected-version check.[^fn-optimistic-version-check] The endpoint executes the modification if and only if the live configuration version matches `config_v7` at the exact instant of write; any version conflict triggers an immediate rejection, returning the task to the agent for re-diagnosis rather than applying an outdated patch onto an altered baseline. Furthermore, to survive network instability, the endpoint implements idempotent request handling: it deduplicates requests using a unique operation identity bound to the caller, target, and payload, storing this identity across a retention window that exceeds the maximum client retry horizon.[^fn-idempotent-operation-identity] The endpoint also exposes a read-only operation-status lookup. These correctness guarantees must reside at the endpoint implementation itself; client tool schemas or client-side metadata can declare invariants, but only the server endpoint can enforce them. Before transmitting the RPC across the network, the runtime appends an intent record for `op_42` alongside its recovery descriptor to a write-ahead journal at the durability boundary chosen for the deployment. Once persistent on disk, the runtime dispatches the request with operation identity `op_42` and expected version `config_v7`.

[^fn-optimistic-version-check]: **Optimistic Concurrency Control**: @kung1981optimistic formalized optimistic concurrency control by allowing transactions to execute without acquiring pessimistic locks, validating at commit time that underlying read sets remain unmodified, and aborting conflicting transactions. The expected-version check adapts this validation to a single configuration record; an abort forces the agent to re-evaluate system state before attempting another mutation. \index{Optimistic concurrency control!expected-version check}

[^fn-idempotent-operation-identity]: **Idempotence**: An operation is idempotent if executing it multiple times produces the exact same system state as executing it once. @helland2012idempotence emphasized that because distributed messaging channels routinely drop, duplicate, or reorder packets, idempotent receiver semantics are a prerequisite for robust distributed systems rather than an optional optimization. An explicit operation identity allows the receiving endpoint to detect duplicates, while a bounded retention window defines the interval during which replayed RPCs can be reliably recognized and filtered. \index{Idempotency!operation identity}

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Deduplication by an operation identity bound to caller, target, and payload is established in @sec-vol3-tool-calling-operation-ids.
:::

At this stage, the configuration endpoint's network response is lost in transit. The client runtime experiences a socket timeout. In distributed systems, a timeout yields no information about execution state: the network may have dropped the outbound packet, the endpoint may currently be executing the transaction, or the endpoint may have committed the write and failed while returning the acknowledgment.[^fn-two-generals-reply] Instead of gambling on a blind retry or prematurely declaring failure, the runtime logs the status of `op_42` as unknown and assigns it to a designated settlement coordinator. Rather than dispatching a second mutating RPC, the coordinator initiates an authorized status query against the endpoint's operation registry. In the successful resolution branch of our scenario, this status lookup confirms that `op_42` committed the requested payload, transitioning the database configuration to `config_v8`. The immutable operation identity firmly binds this remote confirmation to our local dispatch record, resolving network ambiguity even if the original RPC suffered significant transmission delays. Conversely, if the status lookup returns an empty record or encounters a transient service outage, the coordinator cannot conclude that the mutation failed; the original request might still be queued in an intermediate network buffer. In that unresolved branch, the operation status remains unknown, preserved as an open engineering obligation for the settlement owner rather than swept away by process termination.

[^fn-two-generals-reply]: **Two Generals Paradox**: @gray1978notes articulated the classic two generals problem, establishing that no finite message exchange over an unreliable channel guarantees common knowledge between distributed parties. When an RPC reply is lost, the client cannot infer the remote server's state; local timeout heuristics cannot prove whether `op_42` committed, aborted, or remains in flight. Only an explicit query against the service endpoint's durable journal can resolve the ambiguity. \index{Two generals problem!lost response}

Confirming that `config_v8` committed settles the mechanical outcome of the mutation, but it does not resolve the operational incident. The runtime context manager flushes the stale `config_v7` snapshot and assembles fresh post-mutation telemetry to evaluate database performance under live load. Assume that latency percentiles and error budgets gathered across an observation window, `health_window_42`, successfully satisfy the quantitative performance thresholds specified in `incident_contract_v1`, and that secondary policy assertions pass. An authorized human principal or automated gatekeeper evaluates this telemetry and signs `acceptance_42`. This acceptance record explicitly binds together the original incident contract, the operator approval, the settled operation identifier, the new active configuration hash, and the validated metric window. Only then is the incident formally closed under contract for the evaluated duration, with residual monitoring obligations handed off to `operations_owner_42`.

@Fig-vol3-trajectory-lifecycle diagrams this end-to-end systems architecture: a top-level task contract governs the core execution loop (context assembly, model inference, tool calling, and sandboxing), an enclosing harness enforces budgets, approval gates, and durable logs at every step, and final acceptance binds to scoped external evidence, with learning and multi-agent scaling depicted as optional downstream lifecycle extensions.

::: {#fig-vol3-trajectory-lifecycle fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**One Trajectory Through the Whole System**: An adopted task contract (Part VII) governs a live loop in which context assembly (Part II) feeds a model call (Part I) whose proposal becomes a validated, authorized tool call run in a sandbox (Part III), with the observation returning to context as data. The harness (Part IV) wraps every step with budgets, the approval gate, the durable log, and recovery. Acceptance rests on scoped external evidence rather than the agent's report; learning (Part V) and scale (Part VI) are optional lifecycle choices." fig-alt="Layered diagram. A red box at the top labeled Task contract, adopted by an authorized owner, lists goal, environment, permitted actions, observations, and completion criteria and carries a Part VII badge. An arrow leads down to a card labeled Live loop, one trajectory, seconds to hours, containing four boxes left to right: Context assembly (Part II), Model call (Part I), Tool call (Part III), and Sandbox (Part III), joined by arrows, with a dashed arrow from the sandbox back to context assembly labeled observation returns as data. A purple strip inside the card, Harness around every step (Part IV), lists budgets and approval gate, durable log and resume, compensation and loop detection, and the trajectory record. Below the card an Acceptance box (Part IV) reads scoped evidence, not the agent's report, and lists settled outcome, measurement window, policy checks, and authorized adopter. A dashed arrow labeled curated records, if chosen leads to a dashed Learning card marked optional (Part V) reading separate admission, fine-tune, optimize against verifiers. A dashed Scale card marked optional (Part VI) reads split only when the coordination tax pays, and price and provision per accepted task."}
![](images/svg/capstone_trajectory_owners.svg){width="100%"}

The audit chain summarized in @tbl-vol3-capstone-owners enables an independent auditor or site reliability engineer to reconstruct the causal lineage of the incident without relying on a language model's retrospective self-report. Structured records expose operational gaps immediately: a successful completion token from a model call cannot settle the network status of `op_42`, and an unanchored telemetry snapshot lacking a verified observation window cannot validate an acceptance claim.

| **Transition**                 | **Owner**                                            | **Record it leaves**                                                                     |
|:-------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Task admitted                  | Runtime under the delegated contract                 | `incident_42`, `incident_contract_v1`, limits, and `read_scope_42`                       |
| Evidence selected              | Context manager and diagnostic tools                 | `context_manifest_42` with source, version, time, and omissions                          |
| Change proposed and approved   | Model proposes; authorized operator decides          | `change_request_42` and its bound `approval_42`                                          |
| Change admitted and dispatched | Runtime action gate and operation journal            | Durable `op_42` intent, recovery descriptor, and dispatch record                         |
| Lost response reconciled       | Settlement owner querying the configuration endpoint | Source outcome for `op_42`, confirming `config_v8` or preserving uncertainty             |
| Incident accepted              | Designated accepting principal with runtime checks   | `acceptance_42`, `health_window_42`, and residual duty assigned to `operations_owner_42` |

: **Owners and Records Along One Trajectory**: The incident's consequential transitions remain auditable through explicit owners and linked records. An unresolved outcome remains a recorded obligation rather than disappearing when execution stops. {#tbl-vol3-capstone-owners tbl-colwidths="[28,34,38]"}

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Indirect prompt injection, delivered through an observation the agent reads rather than by the interacting user, is established in @sec-vol3-security-injection-entry-points.
:::

In our incident scenario, an attempted exfiltration collides with layered architectural barriers. If the manipulated model emits a tool call directed to an unauthorized external IP address, the runtime action gate blocks dispatch because the destination falls outside `read_scope_42`. Simultaneously, the underlying container sandbox enforces kernel-level network egress filters, dropping unsanctioned outbound sockets regardless of what code or parameters the agent generates. Read operations demand equal vigilance: an adversary might attempt to pass database connection strings into telemetry queries or trigger side-channel leaks through diagnostic error messages. Allowing unrestricted outbound network connections would create an exfiltration channel even if local filesystems are mounted read-only. Layered isolation constraints strictly bound the blast radius of a successful injection, preventing prompt corruption from escalating into arbitrary network exfiltration.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Network egress enforcement placed outside the guest's control boundary is established in @sec-vol3-sandboxes-egress-enforcement.
:::

When the action gate intercepts an unauthorized or malformed action, it appends the rejection event to the audit journal as an undispatched intent. If an operation has already crossed the network boundary into production, terminating the sandbox process does not neutralize the external state change. The designated settlement and incident-response owners must inspect the audit log, determine what side effects materialized in production, and select the appropriate compensatory action. Similarly, if an adversarial prompt causes the model to hallucinate a claim that cluster latency has normalized, the runtime ignores the assertion; model output can never substitute for empirical telemetry verified across `health_window_42`. Rigorous ownership boundaries govern adversarial attacks and standard component outages with equal fidelity.

The remediation trajectory terminates cleanly using a single model and a single runtime controller. Mining this execution trace for offline post-training or delegating sub-problems across a fleet of specialized sub-agents represent subsequent, optional architectural decisions (@sec-vol3-conclusion-seams, @sec-vol3-conclusion-adaptation). Neither optimization alters the authorization invariants required to dispatch `op_42` or the empirical evidence demanded to seal `acceptance_42`.

## Workload Contract Specification {#sec-vol3-conclusion-envelope}

When an automated latency alert fires for `incident_42`, the runtime dispatches a diagnostic workflow rather than an open-ended authorization to modify the production database. An unconstrained optimization loop might easily restore query throughput by disabling secondary index updates or relaxing data integrity constraints, destroying durability in the name of speed. The deployment therefore grounds this remediation workflow in `incident_contract_v1`, an adopted task contract that separates the desired service outcome from the permitted mechanisms an agent may use to pursue it.

### The incident's five-part contract {#sec-vol3-envelope-contract-formalism}

The five contract components define the operational perimeter for this workload. Rather than describing an abstract agent architecture, they bind a specific incident to an identified service, explicit permission boundaries, and named decision authorities. @Tbl-vol3-contract-decomposition instantiates this contract for our database remediation scenario.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The five-part task contract governing an agentic workload is established in @sec-vol3-intro-five-part-contract.
:::

| Contract field                                   | Incident-specific commitment                                                                                                                                    | Owner or supporting record                                               |
|:-------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Goal, $\LongmessageGapPerByte$                   | Restore acceptable query latency for `db_primary_01` without violating the required error-rate and change-policy conditions; leave unrelated settings unchanged | `incident_contract_v1`, adopted by the authorized task owner             |
| Environment, $\Environment$                      | Operate on the identified live service; treat `config_v7` as the expected baseline, not as a promise that the service remains unchanged                         | Configuration source and its versioned operation interface               |
| Permitted actions, $\PermittedActions$           | Initially perform diagnostics under `read_scope_42`; apply the exact proposed settings only after the required current approval and dispatch checks             | `change_request_42`, `approval_42`, and the runtime's action gate        |
| Available observations, $\AvailableObservations$ | Return authorized, bounded diagnostic results with source, version, capture time, and omission information                                                      | Tool result records and `context_manifest_42`                            |
| Completion criteria, $\CompletionCriteria$       | Confirm the authorized operation's outcome, the required service metrics over the stated window, and the applicable change-policy checks                        | `op_42`, `health_window_42`, and the adopted decision in `acceptance_42` |

: **The Incident Contract**: The same five components connect this delegated task directly to its operational permissions, evidence records, and accountable owners. Merely identifying a record name does not establish that its underlying validation checks have passed. {#tbl-vol3-contract-decomposition tbl-colwidths="[23,48,29]"}

A production goal must encode process constraints alongside target metrics because the validity of an outcome depends on how the system reaches it. In this remediation trace, that dependency surfaces through explicit approval bindings and version preconditions. The contract enforces these preconditions at the infrastructure layer: a configuration endpoint that lacks an atomic compare-and-swap or expected-version check cannot safely host this workflow, regardless of how frequently the agent runtime re-reads `config_v7` before issuing a mutation. Without atomic validation at the service boundary, concurrent writes can slip between the runtime's final read and the update, silently overwriting live state.

Observation boundaries constrain read-only diagnostics just as strictly as write operations. Under `read_scope_42`, the agent may query telemetry from designated endpoints but cannot inspect customer database rows, application payload logs, or external network destinations. Tool outputs must also enforce truncation and redaction budgets: the harness captures vital status lines, flags truncated payloads explicitly in the telemetry stream, and routes full raw diagnostic output to an isolated log sink with an independent retention policy. Simple heuristic filters—such as stripping known API keys or ANSI escape sequences—mitigate obvious hygiene hazards, but they cannot prove that an arbitrary output string is free of sensitive data or indirect prompt injections. Reliable protection requires structural access boundaries: enforcing what the agent can read, where intermediate context flows, and which endpoints may receive its output.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Head-and-tail byte budgets and explicit truncation notices for tool output are established in @sec-vol3-tool-calling-bounded-capture.
:::

### Exposures and envelope bounds {#sec-vol3-envelope-four-questions}

An H·S·A analysis identifies the concrete operational obligations generated by this contract. Diagnostic investigation demands strict, finite allowances for foundation model inference and tool invocations. Interacting with live service state and maintaining durable audit trails require source-aware state tracking. Finally, transitioning from diagnostic reads to active production modification requires an explicit escalation of authority. The workload contract fixes these obligations; engineers then select the infrastructure mechanisms needed to satisfy them—determining sandbox boundaries, retry budgets, and model serving configurations.

The operational envelope attached to `incident_contract_v1` applies the harness's trajectory budgets and resource ceilings. This envelope establishes hard caps on agent turns, wall-clock duration, observation buffer sizes, ephemeral disk allocation, and monetary expenditure. Crucially, the execution harness must reserve the bounded liability of every admitted model call or tool operation in advance, while retaining an emergency reserve for post-incident health checks and graceful recovery routines. Accounting for consumed tokens alone is insufficient: an inference request currently in flight can consume the remainder of a budget, and asynchronous tool routines accumulate cloud compute and storage costs even when no model generation is active. The envelope must therefore distinguish between local resource ceilings enforced by the executor and supervisor-level thresholds that halt task admission and trigger automated operator intervention.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Multi-dimensional budget vectors and the advance reservation of each admitted call's liability are established in @sec-vol3-controlplane-accounting.
:::

Similarly, the contract lists idempotency, request deduplication, and out-of-band status reconciliation as strict prerequisites before admitting any remediation workload. When a network partition or gateway timeout obscures the fate of a remote call, these guarantees enable the runtime to poll the endpoint for the true state of an operation rather than blindly issuing a duplicate mutation (@sec-vol3-conclusion-execution).

### Operating-envelope decisions {#sec-vol3-envelope-boundaries}

Consider what happens when a remediation run approaches its execution deadline while awaiting completion of an asynchronous database setting update, `op_42`. Extending the timeout simply because the model predicts imminent success violates the envelope contract. Conversely, abruptly terminating the process and marking the operation as failed fabricates an unverified outcome. A robust runtime halts further task admission, logs the expiration event, and preserves both the pending operation identifier and its allocated reconciliation quota. Because remote work often persists across downstream systems after a local client times out, `operations_owner_42` retains ultimate operational responsibility for reconciling the orphaned operation or executing an explicit administrative handoff when the allocated automated budget expires.

System acceptance operates under fundamentally different boundaries than resource accounting. Operating entirely within budgeted turn and token limits does not prove that database latency has recovered; only rigorous downstream verification recorded in the trace can substantiate recovery. In production architectures, mutating service state, verifying health criteria, and closing an incident ticket are distinct operational milestones with separate evidentiary requirements.

An operational envelope succeeds only when its resource limits align with the physical demands of the workload. It must grant sufficient observation capacity to diagnose the underlying fault, reserve adequate compute and network quota to verify the outcome, and specify a deterministic fallback protocol when execution yields an indeterminate state. Tightening an envelope ceiling reduces blast radius but risks making completion criteria unattainable; expanding it grants greater operational latitude but introduces unhedged liability that demands human oversight. Managing these boundaries across an agent's lifecycle requires synchronizing task contracts, context windows, cached state, and dynamic system configurations as each evolves along distinct timelines.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ A worksheet mapping each contract condition to its design obligation and the evidence to record is developed in @sec-vol3-app-ref-arch-profiles.
:::

## State and Evidence Across Boundaries {#sec-vol3-conclusion-memory}

Before an incident mitigation applies a configuration update, `context_manifest_42` selects diagnostic evidence describing `config_v7`. Once the configuration endpoint confirms that operation `op_42` successfully applied `config_v8`, any subsequent prompt that continues to present `config_v7` as active state provides the model with an incorrect basis for its next decision. The earlier observation remains factually true, but its operational role has shifted: it no longer describes the active system, serving instead as historical evidence of the incident trajectory. Tracing this shift across runtime boundaries illustrates how memory architectures must coordinate with action execution and recovery contracts.

### Records and their roles {#sec-vol3-memory-four-layers}

The context manifest records the exact prompt payload assembled for the next model invocation. It curates relevant material from the task contract, live environment observations, and retrieved artifacts, serving as an ephemeral view rather than an authoritative replacement for upstream data sources. The configuration service establishes and owns the applied configuration under its read-and-update contract. Meanwhile, the runtime operation log durably captures the agent's internal decisions and received evidence, including human approval bindings and the settlement status (whether unresolved or committed) of `op_42`. Ancillary systems such as diagnostic vector indices or model-generated incident summaries help locate and interpret these artifacts, but they cannot override primary system state.

These four categories represent distinct operational roles rather than hierarchical tiers in a monolithic cache. An external service evolves independently of the agent harness, and artifacts vary widely in lifecycle: some are ephemeral scratchpads, others persist under formal retention policies, and still others vanish during host failures. Crucially, the operation log is authoritative only for the local events it has durably written; it cannot attest to external system effects that it has not explicitly verified. If a network response is lost, a generated summary asserting that the configuration has been restored provides zero operational proof of success. This scenario directly reflects the distinction between recorded intent and external settlement.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The trajectory log, which records observations and decisions but is not proof that an external effect settled, is established in @sec-vol3-persistence-event-sourcing.
:::

### Evidence refresh and cached computation {#sec-vol3-memory-coherence-invalidation}

When the upstream service confirms `config_v8`, the context assembly pipeline updates the active configuration entry in `context_manifest_42`. It preserves the preceding `config_v7` record if that diagnostic trace is necessary to justify the remediation step. However, any derived artifacts that depend on the superseded configuration—such as diagnostic summaries or precomputed runbook excerpts—require invalidation or re-evaluation, whereas unrelated operational records remain unaffected. If an asynchronous retrieval index lags behind reality, the runtime can issue an authorized direct read to fetch bounded, up-to-date evidence. If direct reads fail or are unavailable, the manifest must explicitly record the omission rather than silently projecting stale data. Explicit tombstones prevent obsolete snapshots from entering the prompt as active state, though fetching the replacement value still requires a distinct read operation.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Withdrawing a staged observation's authority over current state when its source changes is established in @sec-vol3-context-engineering-context-rot.
:::

The serving system evaluates cache validity through an entirely different lens. Key-value (KV) cache tensors computed for prompt tokens describing `config_v7` remain mathematically valid representations of those exact token sequences, regardless of external system state. An upstream configuration change does not automatically evict accelerator-resident tensors by file path or resource identifier. Instead, when context assembly substitutes `config_v8` evidence into the prompt, prefix reuse terminates at the first modified token. The leading unchanged tokens remain reusable under the prefix compatibility rules, whereas all downstream positions require fresh KV computation. This architectural seam highlights the tension between two foundational principles: prefix coherence (principle \ref{pri-vol3-prefix-coherence}) dictates mathematical reuse of intermediate activations, while source authority (principle \ref{pri-vol3-source-authority}) governs semantic freshness. Consequently, a serving cache hit confirms computational efficiency rather than the freshness or validity of the underlying world state.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Reuse of KV state only over an exact token prefix computed under the same weights and execution parameters is established in @sec-vol3-kv-cache-prefix-compatibility.
:::

Evidence refresh is also bound by temporal reality. Source version checks and retrieval pipeline maintenance ensure that the model receives the freshest available snapshot, but they cannot freeze external services while the model deliberates. Because concurrent systems can drift during generation, the execution pipeline cannot rely solely on prompt-time freshness; it must enforce optimistic concurrency checks at the action endpoint when the mutation is applied.

### Provenance and permission {#sec-vol3-memory-provenance-grounding}

During `incident_42`, the runtime platform captures host-level provenance: which authorized endpoint provided an observation under `read_scope_42`, the corresponding source timestamp and version vector, any payload filtering applied, and the exact model request that consumed the data. The runtime separately logs its own policy admission decisions. These host-verified events are fundamentally distinct from the model's generated assertions, such as claiming that a specific configuration rollout triggered the latency alert. The model's reasoning remains an internal hypothesis until substantiated by verifiable system telemetry.

Untrusted data paths, such as prompt injections embedded in external log streams, underscore this separation from the security boundary. Ingesting text from a trusted storage bucket does not endow that text with operational authority or approval status. Provenance tracks the data lineage and origin of tokens, while the security subsystem enforces authorization against explicit, unforgeable capability grants. The agent runtime evaluates permissions against the active execution context and credentials, treating all observed data strictly as passive payload.

### Adversarial evidence within the same task {#sec-vol3-conclusion-adversarial-evidence}

Real production telemetry is rarely sterile; a diagnostic log entry or an issue tracker comment can contain adversarial instructions designed to exfiltrate database credentials to an external server—an indirect prompt injection. This payload enters the agent's context through an authorized diagnostic read, yet the untrusted text inherits none of the human operator's administrative authority.[^fn-confused-deputy-injection] While structured provenance tagging and XML delimiters assist the model in distinguishing ingested data from operational instructions, model-level comprehension provides no security boundary. Strong isolation outside the model runtime must govern what an ostensibly schema-valid tool call can execute using legitimate system privileges.

[^fn-confused-deputy-injection]: **Confused Deputy**: @hardy1988confused identified the confused deputy problem, in which a privileged service (such as a system compiler) is manipulated via untrusted client input into abusing its legitimate authority on behalf of an unauthorized entity. Indirect prompt injection reproduces this classic failure mode by embedding instructions within retrieved text [@greshake2023not], tricking an agent into wielding its operator-granted authority to carry out an adversary's intent. Robust enforcement systems therefore tie every action to an explicit capability grant rather than inferring authority from the textual context that prompted the call. \index{Confused deputy!prompt injection}

### Cross-subsystem seams and ownership {#sec-vol3-conclusion-seams}

The source-to-context example exposes a fundamental failure mode in modular architectures: storage and serving subsystems can both operate strictly within their local specifications while the agent as a whole acts on stale, invalid evidence. @Tbl-vol3-seams extends this ownership analysis to five critical subsystem seams encountered during the incident. The final two rows govern scenarios where the architecture incorporates continuous learning or delegated multi-worker execution.

| Seam                                     | Incident-specific failure                                                                                       | Principles that meet here                                                                                                                             | Owner and required record                                                                                                                                                    |
|:-----------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| World and its representations            | `config_v7` is presented as current after `config_v8` is confirmed                                              | Source authority (principle \ref{pri-vol3-source-authority}) against prefix reuse (principle \ref{pri-vol3-prefix-coherence})                         | Context and retrieval owners preserve source/version bindings in `context_manifest_42`; the action endpoint enforces the expected version when applying a change             |
| Proposal to effect                       | A lost reply is treated as failure, leading to an unsafe repeat of `op_42`                                      | Intent before effect (principle \ref{pri-vol3-intent-before-effect}), then settlement before retry (principle \ref{pri-vol3-exactly-once-settlement}) | Action and recovery owners retain the admitted intent, operation identity, and unresolved status until the endpoint contract supplies adequate outcome evidence              |
| Recovery and authority                   | A recorded recovery plan is treated as permission to apply a corrective change to a now-different service       | Compensation (principle \ref{pri-vol3-intent-before-effect}) against the typed action contract (principle \ref{pri-vol3-strict-action-abi})           | Recovery owner retains the descriptor and residual duty; any corrective action needs current authorization and applicable preconditions                                      |
| Recorded incident to learning, if chosen | Acceptance of the incident makes every step a training target, or the release grader becomes a selection reward | Release evidence (principle \ref{pri-vol3-release-evidence}) against the verification asymmetry (principle \ref{pri-vol3-verification-asymmetry})     | Curation and evaluation owners separately admit `training_record_42`, preserve its permitted use and evidence limits, and protect release evaluation from adaptive selection |
| Across workers, if delegated             | Diagnostic workers duplicate a consumable allowance or their agreement is treated as independent confirmation   | Coordination tax (principle \ref{pri-vol3-coordination-tax}) against delegated admission (principle \ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-encapsulation})          | Delegating runtime records scoped assignments and reservations; the integration owner checks returned evidence and retains unresolved child obligations                      |

: **Incident seams, principles, and owners**: Each boundary needs both an owner and a record that preserves the distinction the next subsystem relies on, and at each one two principles meet or pull against each other. Local success alone does not establish the end-to-end task result. {#tbl-vol3-seams tbl-colwidths="[15,25,24,36]"}

Delegation makes the final row concrete without altering the acceptance contract. A worker may receive a subset of `read_scope_42` while the parent retains its broader read permissions. That reusable capability differs fundamentally from a consumable allowance: concurrent workers must coordinate reservations against a shared budget rather than each receiving an independently spendable quota (principle \ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-encapsulation}). Similarly, consensus among multiple diagnostic workers cannot substitute for empirical verification. When workers process identical noisy inputs or observe one another's intermediate reasoning, their failures correlate; apparent agreement often reflects shared bias rather than independent confirmation. Whether delegation yields a net benefit is the central evaluation question examined in @sec-vol3-conclusion-adaptation, which balances task decomposition against the coordination tax (principle \ref{pri-vol3-coordination-tax}) incurred across subagent boundaries.

Taken together, structured boundary records enable an auditor or post-incident review to reconstruct exactly what the runtime observed, what operations it proposed, what authority it possessed, and what state the external world ultimately committed. Converting this body of recorded evidence into an admissible next action—whether settling an ambiguous inflight request or dispatching a compensating repair—forms the core responsibility of the execution and recovery boundary.

## Execution Harness Synthesis {#sec-vol3-conclusion-execution}

When an execution trace resolves a lost response with a single status query, it succeeds only because every piece of state the query required was already persisted before the network dropped the reply. The execution boundary is where systems enforce this ordering. Simply selecting a source version or generating an approval record produces no physical side effects on its own. This boundary must explicitly bind an abstract intent, such as `change_request_42`, to the concrete mutation that an external endpoint actually applies—without inventing either success or failure when network visibility collapses.

### Durable intent before dispatch {#sec-vol3-execution-pipeline-stages}

Before transmitting any side-effecting mutation across the network, the runtime must record the admitted intent alongside its recovery descriptor (principle \ref{pri-vol3-intent-before-effect}). The intent log binds `op_42` directly to its originating request, cryptographic approval, endpoint API contract, and resource reservation. In parallel, the recovery descriptor details the authorized corrective procedure, the requisite diagnostic evidence and permissions, and designates `operations_owner_42` as the primary settlement owner. Registering this descriptor only after receiving a response introduces a fatal vulnerability: if the response packet disappears in transit, the runtime is left with an active remote mutation but no durable record of who must reconcile it.[^fn-write-ahead-intent]

[^fn-write-ahead-intent]: **Write-Ahead Logging**: Database recovery methods such as ARIES [@mohan1992aries] force a log record describing an update to stable storage before the update reaches the data it changes, ensuring that recovery can always redo or undo logged operations. Recording `op_42` before network dispatch applies the same ordering to external effects, with a critical systems distinction: the runtime cannot unilaterally redo or undo an endpoint's mutation. It can only discover the true state by querying the endpoint directly. \index{Write-ahead logging!intent record}

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Durable intent, the admitted operation acknowledged by storage that survives the declared failure domain before dispatch, is established in @sec-vol3-persistence-wal.
:::

Durable acknowledgments must cover the failure domain declared by the deployment environment. A local `fsync` on a single host is not a guarantee that the record will survive the loss of the physical storage device or a host-level crash before replication completes. If the required storage acknowledgment is missing or ambiguous, the execution gate must withhold dispatch. Even after an intent is acknowledged to disk, an administrative pause or authority revocation can safely withhold the unsent request, because recording intent commits the system to track the operation, not to execute it unconditionally.

### Lost responses and unresolved operations {#sec-vol3-execution-sagas}

When a network timeout interrupts dispatch, neither the timer expiration nor the surviving intent log can differentiate among the three fundamental failure states: the request dropped before reaching the endpoint, the endpoint executed the change but dropped the reply, or the endpoint crashed mid-execution. Recovering from this branch depends entirely on endpoint guarantees, which must reside at the remote service because the agent's local log and the external configuration service cannot participate in a single atomic transaction. Issuing an idempotent status query rather than dispatching a fresh mutation enforces settlement before retry (principle \ref{pri-vol3-exactly-once-settlement}). Once correlated evidence confirms that the endpoint applied `config_v8`, dependent tasks may safely consume the result. Any subsequent replay of the same operation must conform to the endpoint's repeat contract and pass active admission checks.

@Tbl-vol3-execution-pipeline-stages distinguishes boundary states that naive agent architectures often treat as interchangeable tool errors.

| Evidence at the boundary                                          | What the runtime may conclude                                               | Continuation and owner                                                                                           |
|:------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Current admission fails before this attempt is released           | This attempt was withheld through the gate; earlier attempts are unaffected | Record rejection and its reason; reconsider only under current authority                                         |
| `op_42` intent survives, but its response is lost                 | The external outcome remains unknown                                        | Withhold dependent mutation; `operations_owner_42` retains reconciliation and outstanding liability              |
| Correlated status evidence establishes application as `config_v8` | This operation's effect is established under the endpoint contract          | Record settlement evidence; obtain the service-health evidence required for acceptance                           |
| Status remains unavailable within the follow-up allowance         | Automated reconciliation has not established the outcome                    | End this continuation as unresolved; retain the operation, evidence, reservation, and acknowledged handoff owner |
: **Execution Evidence and Continuation**: Local rejection, uncertain delivery, and established application support different decisions. Closing a continuation does not close an unresolved external obligation. {#tbl-vol3-execution-pipeline-stages tbl-colwidths="[31,31,38]"}

Confirming that an endpoint applied a change still leaves the acceptance step of the trace incomplete; the runtime must verify downstream service health before declaring success. Furthermore, operational costs and financial liabilities incurred by the operation often settle on schedules that decouple entirely from the latency of the underlying mutation.

### Recovery and stopping obligations {#sec-vol3-execution-watchdog}

When an applied change requires remediation, the registered recovery descriptor provides an explicit compensation plan rather than an inverse operation guaranteed to rewrite history (principle \ref{pri-vol3-intent-before-effect}). A corrective configuration request requires active credentials, relevant approvals, and explicit preconditions verified against the live environment—the same strict admission checks that the typed action contract (principle \ref{pri-vol3-strict-action-abi}) enforces on forward actions. Compensations can themselves stall or fail partially. Rolling back a local workspace cannot reverse an external configuration change, just as issuing a network cancellation request cannot guarantee that the remote endpoint terminated execution. All residual obligations remain assigned to `operations_owner_42` until an authorized human operator or automated successor explicitly acknowledges the handoff.[^fn-saga-compensating-action]

[^fn-saga-compensating-action]: **Sagas**: @garciamolina1987sagas proposed splitting a long-lived transaction into a sequence of local transactions, each paired with a compensating transaction that semantically undoes its effect when the sequence cannot complete. A compensation is a new forward action that can itself fail, and concurrent observers may see intermediate effects before compensation completes. A corrective configuration request therefore passes through the same admission checks as any forward action. \index{Saga!compensating action}

Semantic watchdog mechanisms and progress monitoring determine when the execution harness must halt ordinary processing to investigate stalls. Detecting semantic livelocks is non-trivial: repeated tool calls and static observations do not definitively prove that an agent is looping, because an asynchronous status query may legitimately return a pending state across multiple polling intervals. To bound the blast radius of heuristic errors, the harness enforces a strict dispatch ceiling on total invocations and token budgets. When an execution hold triggers, the runtime suspends further speculative dispatches while preserving all admitted operations, allowing only separately authorized, budgeted settlement and recovery tasks to proceed.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Semantic watchdogs that detect activity without progress are established in @sec-vol3-sagas-watchdogs.
:::

::: {#chk-19-intervention-ladder .callout-checkpoint title="Auditing the incident's action boundary"}

Each prompt names a failure at the action boundary; decide which record or check must catch it.

- [ ] **Changed precondition**: `approval_42` names `config_v7`, but another operator changes the configuration before application. Which check must prevent the stale proposal from applying, and who may authorize a revised change?
- [ ] **Retry exposure**: The log contains the intent for `op_42`, but no response. If a lost reply hides an applied change with probability $\HiddenDimensionFour$, what fraction of fresh-identity retries duplicate the change, and which endpoint guarantee brings that fraction to zero?
- [ ] **Missing obligation**: A design records its recovery descriptor only after receiving success. Identify the failure interval this leaves uncovered and the record and owner that must survive it.
- [ ] **Unresolved exit**: The follow-up allowance expires while status remains unknown. Which operation, financial liability, and handoff records must remain even though this continuation ends?

:::

Because every failure in this trace is anchored to a defined architectural boundary and an accountable owner, the system log reveals exactly where the next engineering safeguard belongs—a decision that itself requires rigorous diagnostic evidence before deployment.

## Evidence-Based Systems Intervention {#sec-vol3-conclusion-adaptation}

An execution trace allows us to ask a far more precise question than whether an agent simply needs a larger or smarter foundation model. If `context_manifest_42` still presents `config_v7` as current after settlement confirms `config_v8`, the defect lies in stale state selection. If the runtime blindly retries `op_42` because an initial response timed out, the defect lies in outcome handling and the endpoint's recovery contract. Additional pretraining or fine-tuning might shift how frequently the model encounters these code paths, but modifying weights cannot repair a missing state transition or make an unsafe non-idempotent retry safe.

Effective intervention selection\index{Intervention ladder!intervention selection} pairs an attributed failure with a targeted causal remedy. As formalized in the intervention ladder, candidate remedies should be evaluated in order of operational cost and reversibility. Cheap, easily reversible adjustments come first: refining context and retrieval, hardening tool interfaces and schemas, and enforcing deterministic runtime control. Modifying model weights is reserved strictly for residual failures that persist after these structural remedies have been applied—and only when empirical evidence demonstrates that the residual stems from an inherent behavioral weakness. This sequence represents a pragmatic default justified by cost and reversibility, not an inflexible ritual that every failure must climb. An urgent authorization bypass, for example, points directly to a runtime enforcement repair rather than a prompt modification.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The intervention ladder ordering candidate remedies by operational cost and reversibility is established in @sec-vol3-flywheel-intervention-order.
:::

Although an execution trace records what transpired, causal attribution requires an experimental hypothesis test. We isolate the fault by reconstructing the initial input, tool contract, runtime state, and observed outcome, and then manipulating only the suspected causal variable under controlled conditions. For instance, supplying a missing configuration version directly into the prompt verifies whether the issue was an information deficit. Similarly, replacing an ambiguous network timeout with an explicit pending status reveals whether the tool interface misled the controller. Once a candidate fix is identified, engineers must evaluate the repair across the entire affected task suite while running regression checks across unrelated workloads to detect secondary side effects.

@Tbl-vol3-intervention-ladder-tradeoffs connects candidate intervention rungs to the empirical evidence required to justify them. The first three rows represent low-cost, reversible structural fixes; the two training rows modify model parameters; and the final row addresses the distinct architectural decision of task delegation.

| Intervention           | Evidence motivating the change                                                                              | Obligation the change leaves in place                                                         |
|:-----------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Context and retrieval  | Needed facts are absent, stale, or obscured in the actual model input                                       | Validate source versions and preserve current task constraints                                |
| Tool interface         | Arguments or outcome states are ambiguous to the caller                                                     | Enforce authorization and distinguish a rejected request from an unresolved effect            |
| Runtime control        | Budgets, action preconditions, or settlement rules are not enforced at the responsible boundary             | Test enforcement and recovery under the declared failure model                                |
| Supervised fine-tuning | Admitted demonstrations represent a recurring behavior the current policy handles poorly                    | Supply current contracts and evaluate generalization and regressions                          |
| Reward-driven learning | New attempts can be assessed under a useful scoped reward without a demonstrated response at every decision | Protect assessment, inspect reward gaps, and evaluate held-out behavior                       |
| Delegated trajectories | Separate ownership and focused contexts may improve a declared task objective                               | Bound authority and spending, reconcile results, and compare with a capable single controller |

: **Evidence for an Intervention**: A causal diagnosis directs the remedy; no row guarantees improvement or removes the obligations enforced elsewhere in the system. {#tbl-vol3-intervention-ladder-tradeoffs tbl-colwidths="[21,39,40]"}

Adapting model weights reshapes proposal distributions; it never relieves the system of enforcing contracts, budgets, or security boundaries at runtime. Supervised fine-tuning teaches the model to imitate demonstrated recovery paths and structured search strategies, whereas reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards optimizes these behaviors through autonomous exploration. Crucially, both training paradigms must prove their generalization gains on the true deployment distribution. Even a sandboxed, automated reward evaluator can harbor specification gaming or omit subtle edge cases in task requirements.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Reward hacking, which exploits the gap between a verifiable reward and the intended task, is established in @sec-vol3-rlvr-score-intended-outcome.
:::

Delegation occupies a distinct architectural dimension outside the ladder. Partitioning a task across multiple agents alters system topology, ownership boundaries, and communication overhead rather than repairing an individual component failure. A workload decomposed into clear, decoupled subtasks may warrant delegation without any model training whatsoever. When considering delegation, the primary baseline must be a capable single controller equipped with selective retrieval, speculative sampling, and parallel tool calling. Any architectural comparison must account for what multiple independent trajectories actually cost—specifically, the redundant prompt contexts, serialization latencies across inter-agent dependencies, and reconciliation logic that together constitute the coordination tax (principle \ref{pri-vol3-coordination-tax}). In our running incident, spawning independent diagnostic sub-agents to inspect logs can accelerate triage without granting any worker permission to apply state-mutating production changes. That architectural partitioning remains completely orthogonal to whether the underlying model weights require adaptation.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Benchmarking a multi-agent design against a single controller with matched tools, budgets, and concurrency limits is established in @sec-vol3-multiagent-matched-conditions.
:::

Deciding on a systems intervention therefore synthesizes root-cause attribution, comparative evaluation. Crucially, the boundaries of authority and the verification of acceptance must remain external to the agent configuration itself. Once an engineering remedy is proposed, the remaining question is what empirical evidence supports releasing that complete configuration within its declared operating envelope.

## Empirical Safety Cases {#sec-vol3-conclusion-safety}

An incident record links an approved configuration change directly to an observed service outcome. Rather than assuming that this connection implies general correctness, a systems engineer must ask: what operational claims does the record actually substantiate, which enforcement mechanisms make those claims trustworthy, and what residual failure modes remain unaddressed? Answering these questions requires an empirical *safety case*: an inspectable, structured argument establishing that specific safety claims hold within a defined operating envelope, rather than an ungrounded certificate asserting that an autonomous agent behaves correctly under all reachable conditions.[^fn-goal-structuring-notation]

[^fn-goal-structuring-notation]: **Goal Structuring Notation (GSN)**: @kelly2004goal presented a graphical notation for safety arguments that represents the claims being asserted, the strategies that decompose them, the operational context and assumptions under which they hold, and the empirical evidence that supports them. Structuring an argument explicitly uncovers claims lacking supporting evidence or unverified operational assumptions—the exact architectural gaps that @tbl-vol3-safety-case is designed to expose. \index{Goal Structuring Notation!safety case}

In this framework, a *claim* asserts a specific operational property, such as authorization validity or state idempotency. An *argument* articulates the causal chain linking the system architecture and runtime mechanisms to that claim. *Evidence* provides the empirical backing: audit logs, telemetry windows, regression suites, and operator review traces. As the Software Engineering Institute's assurance-case methodology [@lipson2013assurance] emphasizes, merely citing a governance tool or testing practice is insufficient. The case must demonstrate concrete enforcement, verifiable coverage, and direct relevance to the deployed release artifact. Documenting assumptions and counterexamples alongside supporting records gives reviewers the context needed to assess the true boundaries of the argument.

### The incident safety case {#sec-vol3-conclusion-incident-safety-case}

@Tbl-vol3-safety-case applies this structure to the operational trace of `incident_42`. These claims focus strictly on the mediated database modification and its observed outcome, avoiding overgeneralized assertions about agent behavior across arbitrary tasks. The entries combine concrete runtime records with the supplementary validation suites required by a production deployment case; they outline what the safety case must verify rather than asserting that every offline test ran during the live incident itself.

| Scoped claim                                                                                             | Argument and owner                                                                                                                                            | Supporting evidence                                                                                                                                       | Assumptions and residual uncertainty                                                                                                                                                                  |
|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| The mediated change to `db_primary_01` requires approval for the exact request and current preconditions | The action gate checks `approval_42` against `change_request_42`, its target, desired settings, expected `config_v7`, and validity conditions before dispatch | The approval and admission records, together with tests of missing, expired, mismatched, and stale approvals                                              | The argument depends on controlled access paths and endpoint enforcement; an unrelated privileged operator or bypass is outside this particular gate's claim                                          |
| The lost response does not justify issuing a fresh duplicate change                                      | The recovery owner preserves `op_42` and reconciles through the endpoint's operation-status and deduplication contract                                        | Durable intent and recovery descriptor recorded before dispatch; the lost-response status; the later source confirmation that `op_42` applied `config_v8` | The endpoint must honor the stated identity, atomic version check, and retention contract, including delayed requests; unavailable status leaves the operation unresolved rather than proving failure |
| The incident meets `incident_contract_v1` under the recorded acceptance scope                            | The acceptance owner checks the applied configuration, required change-policy conditions, and the declared service measurement window                         | `acceptance_42` references `op_42`, `config_v8`, `health_window_42`, required checks, and the authorized adopter                                          | Measurements cover the named service and window, not every future condition; they do not prove the model's diagnosis, and post-window monitoring remains with `operations_owner_42`                   |

: **An Incident Safety Case in Three Claims**: Mechanisms, records, and assumptions support different parts of the argument. Evidence sufficient for one claim does not automatically establish the others. {#tbl-vol3-safety-case}

An agent's diagnostic report can help engineers pinpoint anomalous telemetry or surface inconsistencies across distributed logs, but it cannot serve as independent proof of its own successful execution. Similarly, recorded operator sign-offs provide valid evidence only when explicitly mandated by contract. Human reviews carry their own failure modes, latency, and cognitive blind spots, requiring the same provenance tracking and scope validation demanded of automated assertions.

### Release evidence and staged exposure {#sec-vol3-conclusion-release-evidence}

Different validation checks address fundamentally different operational questions. An action-gate test exercises deterministic policy enforcement along a single dispatch path, whereas a fault-injection harness evaluates state reconciliation under dropped packets or transient network partitions. Determining how reliably an integrated agent satisfies contracts in production is an aggregate population question. Answering it requires representative task distributions, held-out evaluation environments, and rigorous uncertainty treatment. The statistical cost of that confidence is governed by @eq-vol3-eval-planning-power: because precision scales only with the square root of the task count, halving the minimum detectable difference between two candidate configurations requires quadrupling the evaluation sample size per arm.

Production assessment requires preserving the disposition of every admitted trial at the observation cutoff, including hard timeouts, failed downstream checks, and unresolved outcomes. If an execution path branches into an indeterminate state, the evaluation harness must classify that trial as unresolved, even if subsequent service latency falls within acceptable thresholds. Similarly, verifying operational health for one service leaves pending financial transactions or external side effects unresolved. By explicitly retaining each pending obligation alongside its designated operational owner, the audit trail prevents aggregated health dashboards from obscuring critical unresolved work.

When offline evaluations support staged production exposure, engineering teams must freeze and identify the complete candidate runtime configuration: model weights, context-assembly pipelines, tool definitions, execution harnesses, and the specific validation suites tied to the claim. Before admitting live requests, the deployment protocol must define the eligible workload envelope, canary routing splits, resource limits, and automated circuit-breaker policies. Live canary routing tests agent behaviors under workload conditions that offline benchmarks inevitably omit. However, assigning a small routing fraction does not inherently bound downstream blast radius; asynchronous side effects, queued database operations, and concurrent tool executions continue processing after an operator triggers an emergency stop. Detecting an anomaly, confirming that admission has halted, and settling effects already released are therefore distinct intervals.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Tripwires that stop admission, and rollback that leaves transmitted requests and changed objects in place, are established in @sec-vol3-evaluation-releases-tripwires.
:::

Revoking API tokens or draining incoming canary traffic halts only future dispatches. Requests already acknowledged by downstream services and state mutations already written to storage persist, together with their designated settlement owners. Rather than relying on the fragile assumption that rolling back a container image restores world state, a production safety case explicitly documents these operational limits and defines containment protocols for partially executed work.

### Evidence preservation under policy change {#sec-vol3-feedback-stability}

An incident trace does not automatically belong in a continuous learning pipeline. If an engineer proposes extracting an execution segment as `training_record_42`, training admission predicates govern whether its context, execution targets, access permissions, and provenance satisfy ingestion standards. Crucially, an unresolved or aborted operational trace is not equivalent to a negative training example; mislabeling it as such biases the learned policy. Furthermore, teams must quarantine validation suites and benchmark distributions away from the training loop. Repeatedly selecting candidate policies against the same evaluation set erodes statistical validity [@dwork2015reusable]. This dynamic exposes the core tension between verification asymmetry under optimization pressure (principle \ref{pri-vol3-verification-asymmetry}) and independent release evidence (principle \ref{pri-vol3-release-evidence}): once a verification metric is converted into a training loss or reward signal, it loses its standing as an objective safety assessment.[^fn-goodhart-verifier-target]
